title: The Mac Backup Problem Most IT Teams Don’t See Coming
summary: Mac backup support can hide coverage gaps. Learn what IT teams should look for when evaluating protection for Mac fleets.
body_markdown:
Macs are the primary fleet at more organizations than ever—tech companies, agencies, schools, professional services firms. Apple Silicon and macOS security took care of that shift. But ask around, and you’ll find the tools protecting those machines usually weren’t built for them.


That’s not a knock on any one vendor. It’s structural. Backup software grew up as a Windows category. Mac support got added later, mostly because customers demanded it, not because anyone designed for macOS from day one. And “supports Mac” on a spec sheet tells you almost nothing about whether a tool actually holds up on a Mac fleet.


Here’s what that gap costs, in actual numbers:


- 43% of IT teams don’t back up all their endpoints
- 58% of organizations had a data loss or security incident in the last year
- 31% cite lack of time and resources as their top challenge protecting endpoints
- Only 9% say restoring from backup is “very easy”


Put those together and a pattern shows up: the data most worth protecting—the stuff living on laptops that never touch a shared drive—is also the data most likely to fall through the cracks.


Why does this keep happening on Mac fleets specifically? A few reasons, and they compound:


- Ported clients, often built on Java or Electron, don’t play well with macOS scheduling. They compete for resources with whatever the user has open, and get disabled.
- Every macOS release changes something under the hood. A tool that isn’t tracking Apple’s developer releases closely takes time to catch up, and catching up can mean missed files or silent failures.
- Mac-first IT teams live in Jamf, Kandji, Addigy, and Intune. A backup tool that needs manual steps to deploy through those platforms wasn’t built for how those teams actually work.
- Pricing models matter too. When backup is metered by the gigabyte, the instinct is to exclude the largest files, which are usually the hardest ones to recreate.


None of this shows up on a feature comparison sheet. It shows up six months later, during an offboarding, a ransomware incident, or an audit, when someone goes looking for a file that was supposed to be backed up and finds nothing.


We put together a white paper that goes deeper: what actually separates a Mac-native client from a ported one, what zero-touch deployment looks like when it’s done right, why per-GB pricing quietly shapes what gets protected, and the specific questions worth asking any vendor before you commit to one.
